title: Same Exam, Different Starting Lines: What A-Level Results Tell Us About Educational Inequality
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes uses UK A-level results day 2026 to argue that a standardised exam does not produce a fair comparison when the eighteen years leading up to it were profoundly unequal. She cites the headline numbers — 28.3% of England's A-level grades at A/A*, ranging from about 23% in the North East to 32.7% in London, and roughly half of independent-school entries at A/A* versus about 26-27% at comprehensives and FE colleges — to show the gap is regional and structural, not a matter of individual effort. Drawing on Education Policy Institute and Education Endowment Foundation research, she traces the disadvantage gap back to a 4.6-month deficit already present by the end of Reception, arguing that by the time pupils sit A-levels much of the outcome has already been set by GCSE attainment, housing, poverty, and school access years earlier. London's strong results despite high deprivation serve as her counterexample that regional inequality is not inevitable, which she credits to sustained investment, teacher supply, and higher pay rather than any single cause. Hughes closes by grounding the argument in her own biography — sitting her A-levels while homeless and working night shifts with no family support — and proposes judging progress not by how many students earn top grades but by how poorly a child's postcode, family income, and school type predict their results.
points: England's 2026 A-level results ranged from about 23% A/A* grades in the North East to 32.7% in London on a national average of 28.3%, and the regional gap has widened since before the pandemic.

More than half of independent-school A-level entries earned A/A*, against roughly 26-27% at comprehensive and FE/sixth-form settings, but Hughes argues this largely reflects which pupils arrive at these schools rather than what happens once they're there.
Disadvantaged children are already about 4.6 months behind peers by the end of Reception, per EPI/EEF research, meaning much of the eventual A-level gap is effectively set a decade before sixth form.

London's combination of high deprivation and strong results is offered as evidence that regional inequality isn't fixed, attributed to the London Challenge legacy, a deep teacher labour market, and higher relative pay.
Hughes proposes a different success metric for results day: not raw A* counts, but how inaccurately a child's postcode, family income, and school type predict their eventual grades.
quotes: In 2026, 28.3% of A-level grades in England were awarded at A or A*. In London, the figure was 32.7%. In the North East, it was around 23%. The regional gap between the highest- and lowest-performing parts of England has grown substantially since before the pandemic.
More than half of A-level entries at independent schools received an A or A*, compared with around 27% at comprehensive schools and 26% at further education and sixth-form colleges.
Research from the Education Policy Institute and Education Endowment Foundation has found that disadvantaged children are already around 4.6 months behind their peers by the end of Reception.

A disappointing result at 18 may have roots in what happened at eight, or even at four. A child who starts school behind, struggles with reading, attends an overstretched secondary school and reaches GCSEs without having caught up does not suddenly arrive in Year 12 with a clean educational slate.

What London has benefited from is sustained efforts to improve schools, including the legacy of the London Challenge. It also has a large labour market from which schools can recruit teachers, as well as higher teacher pay to reflect the cost of living.

I was homeless, working night shifts to pay my own way, with absolutely no support from home. At the time I had a boyfriend with middle class parents, where the biggest thing he had to worry about was United winning at the weekend.

The objective should not be to make every school or region produce identical A-level results. Nor should it be to bring successful private schools, grammar schools or London schools down in the name of equality. It should be to bring everyone else up.
